newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian budget, IMF cash, leave problems in store.
newsitem.headline: Russian budget, IMF cash, leave problems in store.

text.p: Russia will struggle to deliver the growth promised in its 1997 budget and low tax revenue will be a persistent headache despite last week's vote of confidence from the International Monetary Fund, analysts said on Monday.

They said the State Duma lower house of parliament's adoption of the budget at a first reading on Sunday and the IMF decision to release a tranche of its $10 billion loan were positive but not a signal of fundamental economic turnaround.

"It is quite clear that the problems that have been facing the government this year in terms of revenues and non-payments are unlikely to improve significantly unless something fundamental changes," said Roland Nash, chief economist at Renaissance Capital.
The IMF said last Friday it had decided to resume lending to Russia and released some $336 million, citing Moscow's "improved revenue performance".

The Fund had delayed two tranches of the three-year Extended Fund Facility because of concern over poor tax collection. But in recent weeks, the government has put tax debtors under the lash, threatening huge non-paying companies with bankruptcy.

In a further boost for Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's government, the Duma on Sunday passed at first reading a 1997 draft budget which envisaged a deficit of 3.5 percent of gross domestic product, revenues of 434.4 trillion roubles ($78.44 billion) and expenditures of 529.8 trillion.
The budget foresees economic growth of two percent.
But, despite signs the steep decline in output is bottoming out, analysts said this could be optimistic.
"I think there will be an increase in money going into the real economy but I would be surprised to see two percent growth next year," said one Western economist.
GDP was six percent lower in the first 11 months of this year than in the same period of 1995, the State Statistics Committee said on Sunday.
Nash said Russia's financial fundamentals were far better now than at the start of 1995. GDP fell three percent that year.
He said 1996 was essentially an aberrant year marked by the political uncertainty of a presidential election and the illness of President Boris Yeltsin.
Inflation in 1996 would be around 20 percent, compared with 131 percent year-on-year in December 1995, interest rates were down and the rouble exchange rate has been stable.
"All this is positive and that is what gives one hope of a turnaround next year but Chernomyrdin cannot be sure," he said.
But several analysts said that depite the recent improvement in tax collection, which had persuaded the IMF to pay up, it was doubtful the government could meet 1997 budget revenue targets.

"There is an unrealistic element on the side of tax collection, which will mean that probably all the expenditure cannot be delivered," British economist Richard Layard, who acts as a consultant to the Russian government, told reporters.
Russia's tight monetary policy has contributed to misery for millions of workers, who have not been paid for months by cash-strapped firms. Tax revenue, in turn, is below target.

But Alexei Ulukayev, deputy head of the Institute of the Economy in Transition, said the revenue targets were realistic but that more should be done to restrain social spending through reform of the system.
He said the growth target was also "more or less realistic" but would be insufficient.
"For the recovery of the national economy, we should have growth of something like five to six percent a year for the next 10 years," he said. ($1=5538 Rouble)
